name: Street Custom 'Tombstone' Concrete Block Launcher
description: A pneumatic launcher constructed from salvaged compressed air tanks and steel pipe that fires concrete blocks, bricks, or similarly sized debris at lethal velocity. The Tombstone uses a burst of compressed air to accelerate a rough projectile through a wide-bore barrel, achieving enough velocity to shatter bone and demolish light barriers at close range. Accuracy is abysmal beyond 10 meters, reloading requires manually shoving another block down the barrel, and the compressed air supply lasts for perhaps 6 shots before needing refill. Despite every possible disadvantage, the Tombstone fills a niche in Tier 1 warfare: it uses ammunition that is literally everywhere, and the impact of a 2-kilogram concrete block at 50 m/s is not something that body armor is designed to handle.
specifications:
projectile: Concrete block, brick, or similar debris (1-3 kg)
muzzle velocity: 40-60 m/s
effective range: 3-10 meters
barrel diameter: 15-20 cm
air supply: 6 shots per tank at 150 PSI
reload time: 5-8 seconds
weight: 8-15 kg depending on construction
accuracy: Approximately 1-meter spread at 5 meters
story_hooks: A barricaded position in Tier 1 has been holding off security forces using Tombstone launchers — the cheap weapons are surprisingly effective against personnel, and ammunition is the rubble around them.

A modified Tombstone has been built with a narrower bore that fires steel ball bearings at much higher velocity — it is essentially a homemade cannon and someone is using it to puncture vehicle armor.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist chunk of salvaged industrial machinery—squat, aggressive, purposefully unrefined. The silhouette is dominated by a massive flared muzzle and a bulging compressed air tank forming the stock. It reads as pure function over form: a street fighter's answer to precision weapons.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 85–110 cm | Barrel bore: 15–20 cm diameter | Tank body: 30–40 cm | Width at muzzle: 22–25 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and unbalanced—the bulk of mass concentrated in the air tank rear, making it front-heavy and requiring two-handed control. Feels raw and substantial, not refined.
physical_description.primary_material: Welded steel pipe, salvaged compressed air cylinders (likely industrial grade or scavenged HVAC/pneumatic systems), rough-cast or cut sections joined with visible seams
physical_description.finish: Industrial bare steel with heavy oxidation and surface rust in patches. Worn, scuffed, and dented from field use and impact. Some sections show welding slag and grinding marks. Occasional grease stains and concrete dust residue embedded in seams.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray and rust-brown over bare steel; accent of faded yellow safety stripe or warning paint on the air tank (often worn away or deliberately obscured). No intentional cosmetics—only the patina of street fabrication.
physical_description.grip_texture: Bare welded steel pipe wrapped with electrical tape, paracord, or friction tape for grip. Rough, utilitarian, no padding. May have sharp edges or burrs from amateur fabrication.
distinctive_features: Massive flared muzzle opening—dented and scarred from concrete friction
Visible PSI gauge mounted on the air tank (often cracked or illegible)
Manual air valve and release lever (crude casting, sometimes leaking)
Welding seams and patches across the entire frame
Ejection ports venting excess air pressure with visible scorching
Improvised sight rail or notch filed into the top (if added)
Concrete dust and impact marks around the muzzle face
Possible jury-rigged stabilizer fins cut from sheet metal and bolted on
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: No corporate logos. Hand-stamped initials or gang tags scratched into the tank body. Original manufacturer markings from the salvaged air cylinders may still be visible (industrial codes, pressure ratings). Some units bear owner's name or alias etched or spray-painted.
physical_description.condition_typical: Battle-worn and jury-rigged. Dents, welding repairs, and patches common. Air seals degraded over time, requiring frequent refills. Concrete residue caked in the barrel. The weapon looks dangerous not because of its design, but because of its blatant disregard for any safety standard.
